p.src: Two bosons can certainly occupy the same one-particle state. If that state has wavefunction $\varphi$, the two-particle product is $\Psi(x,y)=\varphi(x)\varphi(y).$ Wavefunctions are ordinary complex-valued functions, not operators or matrices, so their values commute: $\varphi(x)\varphi(y)=\varphi(y)\varphi(x).$ The product is therefore symmetric. The same construction cannot give a nonzero two-fermion state, because antisymmetry would require $\varphi(x)\varphi(y)=-\varphi(y)\varphi(x),$ while the two sides without the minus sign are equal.

More generally, begin with any two-particle wavefunction $F(x,y)$, with no assumed exchange symmetry. Its symmetric and antisymmetric parts are, apart from normalization, $\begin{aligned}F_{\mathrm{sym}}(x,y)&=F(x,y)+F(y,x),\\
F_{\mathrm{asym}}(x,y)&=F(x,y)-F(y,x).\end{aligned}$ The exchange check is explicit: $\begin{aligned}F_{\mathrm{sym}}(y,x)
&=F(y,x)+F(x,y)
=F_{\mathrm{sym}}(x,y),\\
F_{\mathrm{asym}}(y,x)
&=F(y,x)-F(x,y)
=-F_{\mathrm{asym}}(x,y).\end{aligned}$ Adding the exchanged function symmetrizes it; subtracting the exchanged function antisymmetrizes it.

A pair of hydrogen atoms provides the more interesting case. There are four constituent fermions: two identical electrons and two identical protons. Let $x_1,x_2$ denote the electron variables and $y_1,y_2$ the proton variables. The four-body wavefunction must be antisymmetric separately under exchange of the electrons and under exchange of the protons: $\begin{aligned}\Psi(x_2,x_1;y_1,y_2)
&=-\Psi(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2),\\
\Psi(x_1,x_2;y_2,y_1)
&=-\Psi(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2).\end{aligned}$

First antisymmetrize the electron variables: $\Psi_x=
\psi(x_1,y_1)\phi(x_2,y_2)
-\psi(x_2,y_1)\phi(x_1,y_2).$ Under $x_1\leftrightarrow x_2$, the two terms exchange places and the whole expression changes sign. Now antisymmetrize this result in the proton variables. The four-term ordering is fixed by the two successive antisymmetrizations. (This construction also fixes the sign pattern $+,-,-,+$ through the variable-label corrections made during the spoken calculation.)  $\begin{aligned}\Psi_{2H}(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2)
&=\Psi_x(x_1,x_2;y_1,y_2)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}-\Psi_x(x_1,x_2;y_2,y_1)\\
&=\psi(x_1,y_1)\phi(x_2,y_2)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}-\psi(x_2,y_1)\phi(x_1,y_2)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}-\psi(x_1,y_2)\phi(x_2,y_1)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}+\psi(x_2,y_2)\phi(x_1,y_1).
\end{aligned}$ An electron exchange interchanges the first two terms and the last two terms, with an overall sign reversal. A proton exchange does the same. Thus the state has exactly the two separate antisymmetries required of the constituent fermions.

zh: (讲课时间: 00:11:11)  听众提问: 如果氢原子是玻色子，那么是什么阻止两个氢原子被直接放在彼此之上？

p.src: Response: Bosonic exchange statistics do not remove the forces between the atoms. Pauli exclusion among the constituents, together with the other interatomic forces, can make spatial overlap extremely costly. That is different from asking whether the atoms may occupy the same delocalized momentum state. A momentum eigenstate is spread throughout space, so common momentum does not mean ramming the atoms into the same point. Even hard-core objects like billiard balls could obey bosonic exchange statistics: their hard cores would prevent spatial overlap, while bosonic statistics would still allow common momentum occupation.

zh: 回答: 玻色子交换统计并不会消除原子之间的力。组成粒子之间的泡利排斥，连同其他原子间力，可以使空间重叠的代价极其高昂。这与询问原子是否可以占据同一离域动量态是不同的。动量本征态弥散于整个空间，因此共同动量并不意味着把原子撞到同一点上。甚至像台球这样的硬核物体也可以服从玻色子交换统计：它们的硬核会阻止空间重叠，而玻色子统计仍然允许共同动量占据。

The constituent exclusion is visible by testing coincidence directly. If the two modeled electron arguments coincide, $x_1=x_2=x$, Eq. [eq:same-hydrogen-state] gives $\begin{aligned}\Psi_{\mathrm{same}}(x,x;y_1,y_2)
&=2\bigl[
\psi(x,y_1)\psi(x,y_2)\nonumber\\
&\quad{}-\psi(x,y_1)\psi(x,y_2)
\bigr]\\
&=0.\end{aligned}$ The corresponding expression also vanishes when $y_1=y_2$. Fermionic antisymmetry applies to the complete set of one-particle labels; the displayed cancellation concerns coincidence of the arguments retained here.)

p.src:
A moving spin-one-half particle is described by a position-dependent spinor, $\psi(x)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\psi_\uparrow(x)\\
\psi_\downarrow(x)
\end{pmatrix}.$ The quantities $\rho_{\uparrow_z}(x)=|\psi_\uparrow(x)|^2,
\qquad
\rho_{\downarrow_z}(x)=|\psi_\downarrow(x)|^2$ are joint position-and-spin probability densities. Their sum, $\rho(x)=\psi^\dagger(x)\psi(x)
=|\psi_\uparrow(x)|^2+|\psi_\downarrow(x)|^2,$ is the position density. If the particle is known to have been detected at $x$, then the conditional probabilities are $P(\uparrow_z\mid x)
=
\frac{|\psi_\uparrow(x)|^2}{\psi^\dagger(x)\psi(x)},
\qquad
P(\downarrow_z\mid x)
=
\frac{|\psi_\downarrow(x)|^2}{\psi^\dagger(x)\psi(x)},$ whenever $\rho(x)\neq0$. Thus an electron is represented by a two-component spatial wavefunction, with the local spin amplitudes allowed to vary from place to place.

p.src:
For example, $\begin{aligned}
|m=+1\rangle
&=
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
-i\\
0
\end{pmatrix}
\\
\Longrightarrow\quad\langle m=+1|
&=
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&i&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$ The projection amplitude is therefore $\begin{aligned}\langle m=+1|\phi(x)\rangle
&=
\frac{1}{\sqrt2}
\begin{pmatrix}
1&i&0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi_1(x)\\
\phi_2(x)\\
\phi_3(x)
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=
\frac{\phi_1(x)+i\phi_2(x)}{\sqrt2}.\end{aligned}$ Applying the same rule to all three eigenvectors gives the spin-resolved densities. (These formulas complete the projection algebra after the explicit correction that $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ need not be real. Treating them as real would incorrectly erase the interference that distinguishes the $m=+1$ and $m=-1$ densities.)  $\begin{aligned}\rho_{+1}(x)
&=
\frac12\left|\phi_1(x)+i\phi_2(x)\right|^2,\\
\rho_{-1}(x)
&=
\frac12\left|\phi_1(x)-i\phi_2(x)\right|^2,\\
\rho_0(x)
&=
|\phi_3(x)|^2.\end{aligned}$ They satisfy $\begin{aligned}
\rho_{+1}(x)+\rho_{-1}(x)+\rho_0(x)
&=
|\phi_1(x)|^2+|\phi_2(x)|^2
\\
&\quad{}+|\phi_3(x)|^2
\\
&=
\phi^\dagger(x)\phi(x).
\end{aligned}$ If the particle is conditioned to have been detected at $x$, then $P(m\mid x)
=
\frac{\rho_m(x)}{\phi^\dagger(x)\phi(x)},$ provided $\phi^\dagger(x)\phi(x)\neq0$. The general measurement rule is always the same: form the bra of the desired normalized eigenvector, project the actual state onto it, and take the modulus squared. The resulting density retains its position dependence.

The four entries of $\Psi$ are not the four coordinates of spacetime. They are coordinates in the smallest vector space on which this anticommutation algebra can act. There are two distinct twofold structures: the division into $2\times2$ blocks and the two-component Pauli structure within each block. Anticipating the interpretation established below, the four possibilities may be organized as $\begin{array}{c|cc}
& S_z=+\tfrac12 & S_z=-\tfrac12\\ \hline
\omega>0 & (\omega>0,+\tfrac12) & (\omega>0,-\tfrac12)\\
\omega<0 & (\omega<0,+\tfrac12) & (\omega<0,-\tfrac12)
\end{array}.$ The lower row consists of negative-frequency electron states. It is not a row of positrons; a positron will be interpreted as a hole in the filled set of those states.

There are two natural suggestions. Taking another time derivative would decouple the system, but adding and subtracting the two equations diagonalizes them immediately. Indeed, $\begin{aligned}i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\psi_++\psi_-)
&=m(\psi_++\psi_-),\\
i\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\psi_+-\psi_-)
&=-m(\psi_+-\psi_-).\end{aligned}$ Defining $\chi_+=\psi_++\psi_-,
\qquad
\chi_-=\psi_+-\psi_-,$ gives two independent equations, $i\partial_t\chi_+=m\chi_+,
\qquad
i\partial_t\chi_-=-m\chi_-.$ For definite-frequency dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, the sum has $\omega=+m,$ while the difference has $\omega=-m.$ This is exactly the positive- and negative-energy doubling found in the earlier one-dimensional example: the relativistic equation again has positive-energy and negative-energy electron solutions. Thus the block doubling separates into positive- and negative-energy branches. Pure rest-frame states may be written $\Psi_{\omega=+m}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\xi\\
\xi
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Psi_{\omega=-m}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\xi\\
-\xi
\end{pmatrix},$ where $\xi$ is still an arbitrary two-component object.

zh: 将这个填满的海中的一个电子激发到正能态。结果包含一个正能电子和一个未被占据的负能态。移除一个负能量会提高能量，因此空穴具有正的激发能量；由于缺少一个电子，它还带有相反的电荷。这个空穴就是正电子。

p.src: The algebra has therefore produced two consequences at once: positive- and negative-energy branches, which become the particle–antiparticle structure, and a residual two-component structure associated with spin one-half. The striking point is that both emerged from the smallest matrices capable of satisfying the relativistic anticommutation relations. Spin had only recently appeared as an empirical property when this mathematical construction produced particles with spin together with an antiparticle branch; in that historical setting the result was dramatic.

p.src: A hole may participate in transitions. A positron has positive energy because it is the absence of a negative-energy electron. If a positive-energy electron fills the hole, the electron and positron annihilate, but their energy must be carried away, ordinarily by photons. In sea language, an electron has filled an unoccupied negative-energy state. The same release of energy can be pictured as an excited electron in an atom dropping to a lower level: the downward transition emits photons.

u.src: Response: They can move the hole from one level to another. An electron dropping into the old hole leaves a new hole at its former energy, so the initial positron becomes a positron of different energy. The energy difference is carried by photons.

ja: 回答: それらは空孔を一つの準位から別の準位へ移すことができる。電子が古い空孔へ落ちると、その以前のエネルギーに新しい空孔が残るので、初期の陽電子は異なるエネルギーの陽電子になる。エネルギー差は光子によって運ばれる。
zh: 回答: 它们可以把空穴从一个能级移到另一个能级。一个电子落入旧空穴，会在它原先的能量处留下一个新空穴，因此初始正电子变成能量不同的正电子。能量差由光子带走。

zh: (讲课时间: 01:44:39)  听众提问: 为什么这不会产生无休止的向下辐射级联？

p.src: Response: Because energy and momentum must be conserved simultaneously. Those two conservation laws do not permit the unrestricted process. The same issue arises for an ordinary free electron: it cannot simply keep lowering its energy by emitting photons in empty space.

zh: 回答: 因为能量和动量必须同时守恒。这两条守恒定律不允许这种不受限制的过程。普通自由电子也会出现同样的问题：它不能仅仅通过在真空中发射光子来不断降低自己的能量。
